claims.text: Non-equiatomic HEAs have complex chemical disorder.
The relevant HEA samples can be structured in low-dimensional nanoscale formats near their magnetic phase-transition temperatures.
A machine-learning approach integrating high-throughput DFT and targeted nanoscale experiments can tune the magnetic and magnetocaloric behavior of non-equiatomic HEAs.
Machine-learning potentials can reproduce a DFT-like phase-space distribution while reducing the cost of free-energy calculations.
A predictive model can couple high-throughput DFT or magnetic free-energy sampling with measurements of nanoscale magnetic interactions and microstructure.
Chemical-disorder and nanoscale effects are pronounced in low-dimensional regimes near magnetic phase transitions.
Distributions of magnetic clusters and local atomic arrangements mediate magnetic exchange interactions.
The proposed model would reveal correlations among non-equiatomic composition, nanoscale structural disorder, and magnetic exchange interactions.
Those correlations would enable precise control of magnetocaloric performance through guided composition and processing adjustments.
Model-guided tuning would produce a more optimized and reproducible magnetocaloric response than unguided tuning.
Model-guided tuning could improve magnetic entropy change and control the magnetic transition temperature.
Untuned non-equiatomic HEAs exhibit substantial variability in magnetic and magnetocaloric behavior.
The variability of untuned non-equiatomic HEAs is caused by uncontrolled chemical disorder and nanoscale effects.
The proposed approach is expected to be effective in low-dimensional non-equiatomic HEA systems.
The approach may be less effective for bulk materials or systems in which microstructural control is less important.
Integrating heterogeneous computational and experimental data and modeling nanoscale magnetic interactions may limit the reliability of the inferred correlations.
